head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Letter number i (from 0) goes to key slot i // 8: the first 8 letters take 1 press, the next 8 take 2 presses, and so on
8 keys, each slot depth is one more press
Presses this letter costs in total

p: Total 12. Giving the most frequent letters the cheapest positions (first slot of each key) is optimal, which is why the frequencies are sorted descending. With more than 8 distinct letters the extra ones would cost 2 presses each.

3016.takeaway: Sort letter frequencies in descending order and charge the first 8 letters 1 press each, the next 8 two presses, and so on.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Splits the road into stretches of consecutive potholes
len(g) for g in ... if g
Longest stretches first: each stretch has the same overhead of 1, so longer ones are the best value
Can the whole stretch be fixed?
Partial repair of the next stretch with what is left (needs at least 2)

p: All stretches are repaired within the budget: 6 potholes.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) in the number of stretches.

3119.takeaway: Fix the longest stretches first, since every stretch pays a fixed extra cost of 1; use any leftover budget for a partial repair.

head: Code
What it does

Tries each target value from the maximum upwards (the solution limits the search to this range)
Total number of +1 raises needed to reach t
The smallest element needs the most raises
The largest need does not exceed all the others combined, so raises can be paired up almost perfectly
Pairs, plus one single raise if the total is odd
The smallest element needs more than the rest: pair each raise of the others with it, then the leftover raises are singles

p: The cheapest target is 4 with cost 15. In this case nothing can be paired (the other element needs no raises), so every raise is a single.

3139.takeaway: For each target, raises are paired when possible (the neediest element is paired with the others); otherwise the surplus uses single raises.

3229.takeaway: Look at the changes between neighbouring required differences; every operation fixes two of them, so the answer is half their absolute sum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Splits the word into runs of equal letters; g is each run's length
Number of original strings: each run came from between 1 and g typed letters, and the number of choices for the typed count is g (all lengths are accepted here)
Every original string has length at least the number of runs
Every original string already has length ≥ k
Number of original strings with total length j so far (only j < k kept)
Sum of a range of dp in O(1)
Add a run of between 1 and g letters to a shorter length j − 1 ... j − g
Subtract the strings that are too short

p: `word = aabbccdd` (4 runs of length 2), `k = 7`. `total = 2·2·2·2 = 16`. Counts of too-short strings after each run (length: ways):
The short ones add up to `1 + 4 + 6 = 11`, so the answer is `16 − 11 = 5`.

3333.takeaway: Count all strings as the product of run lengths, then subtract those shorter than k using a DP over run lengths with prefix sums.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Free time before the first meeting, between meetings, and after the last
Moving k meetings can push them together so k + 1 neighbouring gaps merge into one
Slide the window by one gap

p: `eventTime = 5`, `k = 1`, meetings `[1,2]` and `[3,5]`. Gaps: before = 1, between = `3 − 2 = 1`, after = `5 − 5 = 0`.
The best is 2: move the first meeting right against the second one.

3439.takeaway: Rescheduling k meetings merges k + 1 consecutive free gaps, so slide a window of k + 1 gaps and keep the largest sum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of all square areas (overlap counted once per square)
The lowest y and the highest top edge, where the answer must lie
Area below the horizontal line at height h: for each square, side × clamp(h − y, 0, side)
Binary search on the real number h
Less than half is below → the line must go up (lo = mid); otherwise go down (hi = mid)
below(h) only ever grows with h
The answer to the required precision

p: `squares = [[0,0,1],[2,2,1]]`, total area 2, so we need 1 below the line.
The smallest height with at least half the area below is 1.0 (between 1 and 2 the area below stays exactly 1, so the search settles on the smallest such height).

3453.takeaway: Binary search on the line's height; the area below the line grows with height, so find where it reaches half of the total.
